subsubtopic: QUESTIONING OF UNITED STATES CITIZENS AS TO EXPENDITURES DURING VISITS TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday last the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) asked the following question:
Is it a fact that Canadian officials at the border are instructed to question United States tourists returning to their own country, and to ask them how much money they have spent in Canada and what kind of money it has been? If that is the practice, does the minister consider it wise?
Then further:
Will the minister give definite information later as to whether or not it is the practice?
The questions asked by customs officers at the frontier with respect to the amount of money which the United States tourist has left in Canada have no direct connection with customs, but the action is taken by our customs officers at the request of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. Two forms are used to report the replies to statistics, and samples of these forms I will hand to the hon. member. The white form E.49 is used where the tourist has been in Canada less than forty-eight hours and where he has not been given a traveller's vehicle permit. The yellow permit form E.50 carries the request for the information on the reverse side.
The customs officer, on completion of the data, is expected to forward to the bureau of statistics either one form or the other for every United States passenger vehicle leaving Canada. The officers are also cautioned in port instructions that where the operator of the vehicle is reluctant to give the information there shall be no insistence, but in such case the form showing the number of persons in the vehicle and the approximate length of time in Canada must in any event be completed.
The officials of the bureau of statistics place considerable value on these returns, and are of the opinion that if the questions are eliminated they will be at a serious loss in compiling their monthly and annual returns.
The bureau gives me the following information:
"This method of obtaining information on tourist expenditures was inaugurated in 1940. It has worked extremely well. Many thousands of tourists answer the questions. The fact that many thousands do not, indicates the voluntary nature of the inquiry. Fifty per cent answer the question. Without this
Inquiries of the Ministry

information, the bureau of statistics cannot make reliable estimates of tourist expenditures. We would only be guessing.
"The information we obtain is used both by ourselves and by the United States government in connection with balance of payments estimates. We have an arrangement with the department of commerce in the United States which is responsible for balance of payments figures in that country.
"We supply them with information on: (a) the expenditure of Americans entering Canada by vehicle; (b) the expenditure of Canadians entering the United States by all means of travel.
"The United States Department of Commerce supplies us with information on the expenditure of Americans entering Canada by train, boat, aeroplane and: bus. They give out a postcard questionnaire which large numbers of Americans complete and send to the Department of Commerce on their return from Canada to the United States. This inquiry is also on a voluntary basis".

Mr. G. R. PEARIvES (Nanaimo): Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Transport, notice of which I have sent him? speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: QUESTIONS
subtopic: SAFETY OF LIFE AT SEA
subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATIONS OF INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE AS TO KEEPING CONTINUOUS WATCH
speechtext: I am unable to give a specific answer to the question, but I can say that Canada has signed the convention for the safety of life at sea, subject to approval by this parliament. I have not received a detailed report from the head of the delegation, but I am informed that the convention will not become effective until 1951, and in any event it cannot be realized until such time as fifteen countries have submitted acceptance twelve months before the date I have mentioned.

I should like to answer a question asked some time ago by the hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Menary) with regard to certain flax that was sold to the Middlesex Flax Company.
I am informed that the Middlesex Flax Company entered into contracts with certain farmers for the growing of registered and certified flaxseed. The contract price for this flax for seed purposes was different from the commercial price of flax for crushing purposes, which latter has been fixed for the present crop year through the Canadian wheat board. That board's fixed price does not apply to registered and certified seed, which is not marketed through the board.
I am informed also that the quality of some of the seed delivered by growers to the Middlesex Flax Company was below the registered and certified seed standards, and that this flaxseed was delivered by the company in the name of the producers to the wheat board as commercial flax for crushing purposes. The fifty cent bonus has already been paid to these growers.

speechtext: I think the committee should have from the minister some further justification for the power that is being asked for here, because it is apparent that this could be used for purposes that parliament would not intend. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TARIFF BOARD ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TENURE OF OFFICE, APPOINTMENT, ETC.
speechtext: The purpose of the amendment is not such as my hon. friend suggests, but to give a reasonable degree of flexibility. 1 have one board in mind on which a member has served most efficiently for a term of ten years, but his age may now be such that it would not be appropriate to appoint him for a further term of ten years. Therefore it is felt that power should be taken to appoint for a term of less than ten years. In these term appointments it is always a matter of judgment how long the term should be. Personally I think this provision is desirable, and I cannot see how it could be subjected to any abuse.

maintopic: TARIFF BOARD ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TENURE OF OFFICE, APPOINTMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
The purpose of the original ten-year term, as I understand the legislation of 1932, was to assure the members of the board of that tenure of office so long as they discharged their duties. It relieved the members of the board from any fear of removal if they were giving decisions that might not be acceptable to the government of the day. But if you make inroads upon that ride and make the appointments for a shorter period, it seems to me you may defeat the purpose of the original ten-year term, which in addition to giving the board security of tenure, removed them so far as possible from political pressure. This is not purely an academic question, because I think every member of the house appreciates the necessity of keeping the board
free from political influence. By making it a shorter term you run, the risk of invading that principle where a member of the board may be hopeful of reappointment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TARIFF BOARD ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TENURE OF OFFICE, APPOINTMENT, ETC.
speechtext: I really do not think it can be subject to abuse. Primarily it was for the purpose of enabling the government to get competent men by giving them reasonable security of tenure.

maintopic: TARIFF BOARD ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TENURE OF OFFICE, APPOINTMENT, ETC.
speechtext: Does not that same remark apply today?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TARIFF BOARD ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TENURE OF OFFICE, APPOINTMENT, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, but I still think the power should be there. Let us say a man who is sixty-five years of age is still thoroughly competent to carry on his judicial functions. It might be desirable to reappoint him for a further period, but not for a further ten years. I really do not think there is any possibility of abuse by providing flexibility so that appointments may be made for less than ten years.

maintopic: TARIFF BOARD ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TENURE OF OFFICE, APPOINTMENT, ETC.
speechtext: The minister has dealt with the case of reappointment of a member of the board whose age is such that he is not likely to continue to serve for a further ten years. Is the minister prepared to confine it to reappointments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TARIFF BOARD ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TENURE OF OFFICE, APPOINTMENT, ETC.
speechtext: That might be undesirable, because you might want to appoint a man who is in his early sixties but who on account of his age should not be given a full ten-year appointment. I do not suggest that appointments will often be made for less than, ten years, but I do not think you will get first-class men to take these jobs for less than ten years. I think it is a reasonable discretion to give to the executive.

maintopic: TARIFF BOARD ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TENURE OF OFFICE, APPOINTMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Is this board going to be in the future just what you might call a political board with whose decisions the government of the day can interfere? The board was appointed to decide tariff matters, but as a matter of fact it simply forgot its functions from February 1947 right on down through Geneva and then Havana.	An
announcement was made in November of that year by the government of a new economic policy for this country. There were a very large number of applications pending before the board during that time, all of which were held up.
Clause 1 provides for a ten-year appointment. I object to the principle involved in clause 1. I object also to the principle of the government of the day, of its own volition, over the head of parliament when the house is in session, changing the fiscal system of this
Tariff Board Act

country. I have had several complaints from businessmen that they could not get rulings on customs and tariff matters because the board was away in Geneva for eight months in 1947 and then in Havana. The tariff will always be a political question, and no board can change it. If they did, they would be fired or hanged on a sour apple tree. If we are to have a tariff board, let it be a board that will discharge its functions, not one that will be here today and gone tomorrow. What is to become of our trade with the mother country if the board does not discharge its functions?
This board should have looked into the situation in connection with the Canadian international trade fair which has been held in Toronto for the past two weeks. There were many complaints from businessmen in Canada and the mother country which came to light during the fair and should have been looked into by the tariff board. Something should be done to restore the confidence of large and small businessmen in the trade policies of this country.
I object to this clause, Mr. Chairman. I think ten years is too long. Nobody knows what may happen by that time. As Time pointed out, we may be an economic unit of the forty-nine states of the United States. No one can tell what will happen. No wonder there is unemployment and unrest in the country.

Sections 2, 3 and 4 agreed to.
On the title.

maintopic: TARIFF BOARD ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO TENURE OF OFFICE, APPOINTMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Prior to the last war this board did function, and from my observations I would say it did a good job on behalf of Canada. During the war, by order in council, many of the functions of the board were set aside. Now that the war is over we are back to a peacetime economy, and it becomes necessary that we have an organization of this kind in order that proper-representations may be made as to tariffs.
I should hope the board might maintain the record of the late Judge Sedgewick, who was chairman of the board in days gone by. Under his chairmanship I witnessed the common man being heard, with due consideration given to all the people of Canada. One might say that it was their interests versus some of the bigger interests of the country. If the board for which provision is made in the bill functions as it operated in 1935, 1936, 1937 and 1938, prior to the death of the late Judge Sedgewick, I am satisfied it will be a vehicle through

which the people of Canada can be heard. Their representations can be analysed by experts who know what is best for Canada, and under our present economy such an organization is necessary.

There was a lot of discussion on the proposal made last year with respect to the diplomatic superannuation act, and according to the parliamentary secretary no changes have been made since then. It is [Air. Fournier (Hull).]
time we woke up about this particular matter, because this thing is much overdone on the seven seas. Our trade commissioners do wonderful work, but those ambassadors and embassies do little or nothing. We have these embassies all over the seven seas. It is running into a large sum of money now with superannuation; it is a sinkhole for public money. It is all based on the doctrine that we are a first-class nation when we are not. We depend upon Great Britain's supremacy of the seas for our very life.
Now we have the united nations, and a lot of this superannuation is for that. If it was a baseball organization they would call it a "pudding-head" organization, because none of them ever knew enough to touch first base. We will see a sample of this tonight over beside the west block when the hon. member for Fort William is conducting his baseball game. We are not in this united nations organization for fun. It is dividing the whole British empire. The enemy may invade this country, we do not know hoAV soon. They may come sooner than we think.
The people back home in the constituencies are trying to find out what is going on. They are just blindfolded and are allowed to know only as much as some of these columnists let them know-columnists who come in here for a few minutes in the morning and then they all leave and the result is the people do not know what is going on down here; they no longer become enlightened. Yesterday we provided an additional $10 a month allowance for those who fought for us at the hazard of their lives. All they get is that small contribution of $10 a month compared with what we pay for these families of ambassadors.
I am surprised that this country allows an organization such as this to be in existence all over the world. Nobody knows what the expenses are. Nobody knows what these ambassadors are costing this country. We cannot get any information. When a question is put on the order paper it is marked as an order for return and that means that it is dead and buried for the session.
There are a lot of people around here who want to be ambassadors and get the superannuation with it. I have never been asked to be an ambassador, but I think I have done as much to create good will as many other people. Now they are called "Their Excellencies" if you please. Some of them even have uniforms. How can they do that? What is being paid for all this? It must be a fabulous sum.
The people back home are blindfolded, but they reversed the prediction of some columnists in Ontario on June 7 last. Now they have

Diplomatic Service Superannuation Act
another organization-consuls general. The hon. member for Davenport would make a very good consul general. He has been doing this sort of work at his own expense. He has been travelling all over the country in his own car. He gave me a ride last Saturday, and I notice that he needs a new car. With the travelling he is doing for the country something should be done for him.
All this is just a waste of money. We have the ambassadors with their staffs, we have first secretaries, we have second secretaries, we have third secretaries and all that kind of thing. Now they propose to give them and their families all pensions in a special act. This is being done -when people cannot get houses to live in, or even rooms. Here we are pensioning these people and their families. The people back home in the constituencies are getting tired of the two old parties and are voting for something opposite. I know that because I represent these people. Mine is an industrial riding. They had a disaster there last Sunday which shocked me, but nothing was done about it; no columnist in the gallery would say one word about it. Yet these people are suffering.

Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 347, to amend the Railway Act, the Exchequer Court Act and the Judges Act, 1946.
Mr. DONALD M. FLEMING (Eglinton): Without traversing the ground covered in the debate on the resolution I wish to record my opposition to this bill on second reading.
The house will observe that in one bill we are asked to amend three public statutes, which indicates the distance the government is asking the house to go to meet the exigencies of one particular case. I urge, Mr. Speaker, that this is not the kind of bill that this house ought to favour. I mention these reasons without discussing them in

further detail because I think they were adequately developed in debate on the resolution stage.
In the first place, it is wrong in principle to revise or amend no fewer than three public statutes to meet the immediate exigencies of one particular case. This case cannot be of a nature that could justify the extensive revision of three public statutes to meet it.
In the second place, the way the government has gone about this whole question shows what has become a characteristic disregard of the rights of parliament. Parliament's prerogatives have been flouted by the government in its assumption that it can proceed and make all arrangements and announce in advance the appointment before parliament even knew the nature of the legislation that it was going to be called upon to pass to make possible what the government had already undertaken to do in advance.
In the third place, the proposed appointment of a judge as chief commissioner while he continues to hold judicial office in a court, is unsound in principle. It is no answer to say, as the Minister of Justice said in the debate on the resolution, that the board of transport commissioners is a court of record; that judges have held that office in the past; that it was within the contemplation of parliament when the Railway Act was first passed that the appointment of chief commissioner should be open to judges as well as to experienced lawyers. That is no answer. It is perfectly open to the government to appoint Mr. Justice Archibald or any other suitable and qualified person, but it is not proper to continue him in a judicial office while he is holding the office of chief commissioner of the board of transport commissioners.
In the fourth place, the idea of narrowing down the field of those from whom the chief commissioner may be selected to members of the panel of judges of the exchequer court is likewise wrong in principle. Why should the appointment to so important an office be narrowed down to selection from among four or five men who, however eminent may be their attainments in law, however well qualified they may be to hold office in the exchequer court, may not be qualified for the high and exacting responsibilities of the office of chief commissioner of the board of transport commissioners? That simply means that when it suits the convenience of the government to find outside the exchequer court panel a suitable chief commissioner,

Board oj Transport Commissioners
they will bring in legislation to enlarge the exchequer court, using that court as a sort of reservoir convenient to them in making their appointment to the office of chief commissioner. This will not increase respect for the courts, and surely one thing that we have learned in these troubled times is the importance of keeping hands off the judiciary.
Further, and this is the fifth reason, this measure will create anomalies and inequalities within the board of transport commissioners itself. It will mean that the chief commissioner stands in a different position from the other members of the transport board. When his term of office is ended, he is nevertheless assured of a life appointment in the court, if he should not be reappointed to the transport board. That is not a sound position. There is no reason why the chief commissioner, in that respect or in other respects except salary, should be in a more favoured position than other members of the board.
In the sixth place I have already indicated my reasons for saying that this measure will create anomalies within the exchequer court itself. A judge of that court will be in the court but not really of it, because under a section of this bill he is expressly prohibited from exercising jurisdiction of the exchequer court. Is not that an amazing situation? The government will appoint an honourable gentleman to the exchequer court of Canada, but not for the purpose of permitting him to exercise any of the jurisdiction of the exchequer court; for as a matter of fact he is told that though he is appointed to the court he shall not be permitted to exercise the jurisdiction of a judge of the exchequer court.

The government is asking this house to violate principle after principle in order to meet the exigencies of its wishes in this particular case. Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Yesterday, when commenting on my remarks on the resolution, the Minister of Justice, with that genius for accuracy which is his, made some use of the exact or dictionary meaning of the word "political". I recall that when the late Lord Tweedsmuir came to Canada and was asked by reporters who met him at the dockside what he did in private life, he said he was a publisher and politician. This occasioned surprise, which was hardly mild, among Canadians; because rightly or wrongly we have developed on this continent a subsidiary or secondary meaning for the word "political".
I agree that the definition which the minister gave is etymologically accurate, but I think

Board oj Transport Commissioners
he will agree with me that everywhere, possibly with the exception of Nova Scotia, it has a secondary meaning which is not always savoury or not always free from a certain suggestion of cynicism. I used the word in its popular sense and in the way in which most people understand its use in this country. Here I reiterate what I said yesterday. I have nothing but admiration for the hon. gentleman rvhose name has been mentioned for this position, and I suggest that his qualifications as a lawyer and as a man of learning and experience should of themselves be sufficient to qualify him for the high office to which it is the government's intention to call him. But what I object to is his continuation as a judge in his new office. As I have said so frequently in the house, it is unfortunate that the great reputation of the judiciary for fairness and for freedom from partisan influences should be brought into an arena where partisan influences must and do play their part. It may be necessary that we have tribunals whose function is to solve difficulties in which these influences play their part. But I assert, with all the power I possess, with all the faith I have in the judiciary, and with all the desire I have for the maintenance of its integrity, that the judiciary as such should not be subject to these influences.
As a result of these practices, it is now commonly said in some areas: Oh, I do not want to go before that judge; he is a company man; or I do not want to go before that judge; he is a labour man. These assertions result from the use of the judiciary for the solution of extm-judicial perplexities and difficulties which are highly tinged with politics in the ordinary acceptation of the word, and with expediency, something that is entirely apart from the higher plane on which justice reigns or should reign supreme. I can tell the right hon. gentleman that if he were to canvass the judiciary and take a poll of the right-thinking judges-and thank God they are still in the vast majority-he would find that they all deplore the use and exploitation of them and their high office, their integrity and their great reputation, for the solution of political and partisan embarrassments.
It is not necessary to the efficiency of his work that the gentleman whose name has been mentioned here should take to his new office the title and reputation, of the function which he is abandoning. I make bold to state to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is a wrongful use of the judiciary which is held in high repute to enlist its services to make acceptable solutions and decisions which have nothing to do with the ordinary administration of justice.
At a time when people are so uneasy, when

they are not giving the adherence they used to give to the maintenance of the great institutions upon which our whole system of government and civilization rests, it is unfortunate that any of these institutions should be necessarily weakened by exposing a member of any one of them, no matter how distinguished he may be, to popular criticism because momentarily he may be called into a field where considerations other than learning in the law and integrity in the sense of honestly applying that law must prevail. The result must necessarily be a loss of prestige by and damage to the institution. If there were any other reason than the attempt to clothe with judicial authority decisions which of their essence must depend upon accommodation and fleeting and partisan advantage, I would not be so pronounced in an attitude which I hope is expressed in temperate language, although I am greatly disturbed at the necessary result which must follow from a continuation of this practice.
I ask the right hon. gentleman, in the light of events of the last few years-I do not wish to wound or to injure the reputation of any judge in particular; the incidents are uppermost in the minds of all hon. members, and in none more so than in that of the minister- if he does not think that the conduct of the govern,ment taking distinguished members of the judiciary off the bench from time to time and making them the arbiters in matters which are not judicial, which do not depend upon the interpretation of the law, and which do not depend entirely upon justice, has resulted in a loss of status and dignity on the part of the bench and the magistracy?
I cannot believe that there is any lawyer, I cannot believe that there is any judge, who, making a canvass of the events of the last few years, can escape the conclusion that this practice of conscripting the judiciary to settle quasi-political feuds has tended to weaken the respect and the confidence of the Canadian people in the great institution of the law, and in particular in that most important branch of it, the judiciary. For that reason I am opposed to this bill and opposed to all practices which bring the judiciary into the adjustment and settlement of questions which are beyond their scope and which expose the members of the bench to the type of criticism, harmful, unfair, and sometimes cruel, which has been levelled at members of the judiciary who have responded to the invitation of the government to perform extra-judicial duties.

Again, there is this question of the dispensing of justice. I may be wrong, but my understanding is that the judges do not dispense justice. They interpret the law, which may be just or unjust, depending upon how it is drafted. When a judge's decision is reversed on appeal, it seems to me that it is reversed not because he erred in the matter of justice but because he erred in a matter of law. Whether his decision was just or unjust does not enter into the situation at all. The question is whether he interpreted the law according to precedent.
This is a complex bill, and if I had not such profound faith in the integrity of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) and a knowledge of the close study which he gives to matters of this kind, I might be inclined to be more critical of it. In any case I do not know sufficient about its underlying principles to criticize; but I cannot see that there is or could be anything wrong in appointing a judge to any position where there is no interference with his freedom to deal with the questions that come before him, except the restrictions imposed by his own conscience. Surely that is sufficient protection for the judge, whether he is on the bench or on the board of transport commissioners or any other board or commission. I think it is highly desirable that the judges should be kept in as close contact as possible with the economic, social and political conditions that prevail in this country, so that they will be in a position to understand what motivates and compels people to act in the way they do. To take them out of the conditions in which they have lived all their lives and assume that when appointed as judges they can in their virgin purity dispense abstract justice is of course just nonsense.

maintopic: TRANSPORT BOARD

speechtext:
I wish to point out that this section deals with two acts. While the first section, which is numbered as clause 1, deals with an amendment to subsection 2 of section 10 of the Railway Act, which has to do with the question of the appointment of a commissioner, the other two clauses have nothing whatever to do with the Railway Act. They amend the Exchequer Court Act. I suggest that they should be separated. One clause should be an amendment to subsection 2 of section 10 of the Railway Act, and the other clauses should be an amendment to section 6 of the Exchequer Court Act. If anyone wants to know what are the duties of this particular judge, I do not think he would ever find them out by looking at the Railway Act. He would look at the Exchequer Court Act to see what limitations were placed upon the powers of the four judges, one of whose powers is limited by the fact that he can hear only certain cases in the exchequer court. He can carry on in other cases, apparently, save as his duties are restricted. That is why I think the amendment should be made to the Exchequer Court Act.
On several occasions I had to look up certain matters when we were dealing with certain types of legislation, and from the index to the statutes I had a great deal of difficulty in finding what I wanted.
May I point out that some of the duties of the transport board are set forth in the Railway Act. Another act, passed in 1938, chapter 53, also deals with their powers. I must confess that during the recess I had a great deal of difficulty digging out their powers from the two acts. It may be that when the new revision of the statutes takes place the necessary changes will be made; but I suggest that in this, as in all other legislation, an effort should be made to enable a person to find the powers of this board when he looks for them.
Subsection 2a says that section 7 of the Exchequer Court Act shall not apply. That refers to the residence of the judge. Perhaps the minister will have something to say about section 6 of the Exchequer Court Act. That is one reason why all the powers of the exchequer court judges should be in one place. Section 6 of the Exchequer Court Act says:
A judge of the court shall not hold any other office of emolument, either under the government of Canada or under the government of any province of Canada.
That would seem to be in conflict with this proposed legislation which introduces an amendment to the Railway Act. Is it expected

Revised Statutes oj Canada
that the chief commissioner will carry on in the same way as the chief commissioner has done in the past? I feel that this legislation envisages his having some time to devote to exchequer court business. There are six members of the transport board. As the minister points out, their duties have not been so great in the recent past. Is it the intention to rearrange the duties of the chief commissioner? Will he deal only with certain important kinds of work of the board, or is that something which will be left to the board itself? Because some extra time will be at the disposal of the chief commissioner I do not imagine that he will spend all his time at this work. Does the same thing apply to the other members of the board? If so, the time may be fast approaching when there should be a certain overhauling of the transport board so that the time of the members will be fully occupied.

The bill is not a bill to amend the Railway Act only, but to amend three acts, and it naturally has to go in one act; it could not very well go in the whole three.

maintopic: REVISED STATUTES

This commission shall examine the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, and the public general statutes of Canada enacted since the coming into force of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, and in accordance with the provisions of this act shall revise, classify and consolidate the said statutes.

speechtext: There are certain sections which indicate that wide power is being given here. I looked up the word "revise" in the dictionary on the table of the house. Amongst the definitions of "revise" is to look over, re-examine or reconsider and amend faults in various things, including amending faults in the law. Why are there so many words here'-revise, classify and consolidate? The meaning of "revise" must be gained from reading the subsequent paragraphs. Under section 5 "revise" would mean, among other things-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: REVISED STATUTES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMMISSION TO EFFECT REVISION
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: REVISED STATUTES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMMISSION TO EFFECT REVISION
speechtext:
There is only one way in which I can define what "revise" means, and that is by reference to subsequent sections where the powers are given to the commission. It is for this reason that I refer to them, sir. It is merely for the
purpose of indicating how wide the power may be that is now to be conferred by parliament on that commission.
If I may proceed, Mr. Chairman, I would point out that under section 5 the powers that are given-and these are powers as to alterations which must come within the purview of the word "revision" are as follows:
5. (1) The commission in consolidating the said statutes . . . may make such alterations in the language of the statutes as are necessary in order to secure uniformity of style and expression-
That is, in fact a revision-the type of revision that consists in consolidation- together with the removal of language that is unnecessary or that contains grammatical errors and the like. The section continues:
[DOT]-may rectify apparent errors-
So far so good.
-and reconcile conflicting provisions or enactments-
That goes a long way. To "reconcile conflicting enactments or provisions" indicates the granting of a power to decide what in the minds of the commission should be done in order to bring into realignment in accordance with the wishes of the commission two apparently dissimilar sections. The section continues:
-and in cases of doubt or ambiguity the commission may make such amendments as are necessary to resolve such doubt or ambiguity-
I shall stop there for moment. What is that but the power to legislate? What is that but giving power to a commission to say that parliament did not know what it was doing, that parliament did not properly legislate but has left an ambiguity with the result that a change must be made? I feel that is too wide a power to grant to a commission which will finally determine the question without regard to parliament. If this commission were merely to recommend, I could understand such a power. But for this commission to be given by parliament carte blanche to determine finally what parliament meant, goes farther than the question of revision should go. Indeed, parliament in fact delegates to a commission power to do something which the commission says parliament in its wisdom did not properly do. That, sir, is going too far. Actually it means that parliament delegates to a commission of seven the right to decide what parliament should have said and in fact did not say. For the next sentence says-and I again refer to section 5(1)-as follows:
-the commission may make such amendments as are necessary to resolve such doubt or am-
Revised Statutes of Canada

biguity in accordance with what the commission considers to have been the intention of parliament.
That is a wide power. It is actually placing in the hands of a commission, over which parliament will have no control, the power to do that which judges frequently must do, namely, determine the intention of parliament. And in determining that question, judges must depend entirely upon the words used by parliament. In this section, and the subsequent sections defining the meaning of the word "revise", we are actually placing a commission in a higher position than that in which the judiciary of this country today is placed. The judges, when they are determining the intention of parliament, are restricted by the words used. This commission is to have no such restriction at all. I feel that any changes that are made should not become law without parliament actually having the right to decide whether or not those changes should in fact be made.

I rather got the impression from the discussion yesterday that some members felt this was a job for clerks, a sort of scissors-and-paste job. I do not agree. To put the present statutes in proper shape and bring them together requires a good deal of ability.

maintopic: REVISED STATUTES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMMISSION TO EFFECT REVISION
speechtext: Is it proposed to substitute this commission for the high court of parliament? When the Ontario statutes were revised years ago, the work was done by a board, which at one time was under the chairmanship of Chief Justice W. R. Meredith. It was largely a committee of officials, presided over by a judge, and afterwards it was passed on by the legislature. Parliament ought not to delegate its powers and functions to any crown officer-because that is what they all will be, crown officers. Are we to accept their revisions without reading them? Is parliament to abdicate its functions? I am surprised to find a bill like this before parliament, and I protest against it.

maintopic: REVISED STATUTES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMMISSION TO EFFECT REVISION
speechtext:
I wish to say a word or two in relation to parliament's functions in regard to the revision. A comparison of the present bill with chapter 65 of the statutes of 1924 shows that, apart from sections 1 and 2 which we have dealt with and which did not have a counterpart in the act of 1924, the remaining sections of the bill have been taken verbatim from the 1924 act, with the exception of section 5, and the minister has indicated that when we reach that section he proposes to restore the original section. It may be then that we shall be in the position of being asked to legislate in precisely the same terms, with the exception of sections 1 and 2. as those contained in the legislation of 1924. Nevertheless, I think there is still enough breadth in the duties attached to the work of revision as indicated in sections 2 and 5. even after the new section 5 which the minister is to propose, to make it not only desirable but necessary that any changes going beyond what the minister referred to as a seissors-and-paste job should be reviewed by parliament. I do not think parliament will be slow or unwieldy in dealing with matters of this kind. Parliament could move very quickly to appoint a special committee for the purpose of reviewing the statutes as revised by the commissioners, and this committee could come to the house from time to time with the recommendations of the commissioners. But I cannot reconcile my duty as a member of parliament with simply accepting provisions of this kind, in which parliament is saying in effect: We are giving certain instructions to the commission; we fully expect that the commissioners will adhere strictly to their instructions, but whether they do or do not, whether they confine themselves to the terms of those
instructions or whether they stray afield, their work is not to come back to parliament. All they will be required to do is to deposit the roll with the clerk of parliaments. Then, under section 7, on the filing of the roll, power is reserved to bring those statutes into full force and effect.
I do not expect in advance that the commissioners will exceed the terms of the commission. But I do not believe parliament will be doing its duty if it agrees now to accept in advance whatever work the commissioners may do, and whatever may appear on the roll which they will deposit with parliament perhaps three, four or five years hence, when their work is completed. I do not think that is the way in which parliament ought to address itself to its responsibilities. At this stage we have to insist that there be some limitations in the terms of the bill, so that in respect of anything other than what the minister has described as the scissors-and-paste job of consolidation, parliament will accept responsibility and will have an opportunity of reviewing the work of the commissioners.
I do not conceive that that will mean delay, or that parliament will make any unwieldy or cumbersome interference with the work of revision. As I have said, parliament can set up a committee which will make its recommendations to the house. It seems to me parliament must accept its responsibilities and its task in connection with this work of revision.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REVISED STATUTES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMMISSION TO EFFECT REVISION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I had any faith in the possibility of the committee, of which my hon. friend speaks, considering over again all the statutes of Canada, I would perhaps accept his suggestion. But I know perfectly well that the committee would not do that. The thing to do is to do what has been done repeatedly in the past. Instead of relieving these people from responsibility we should place the responsibility upon them, so that they may do a workmanlike job. They have always done it in the past, and they will do it in the future. If we argued a week on each statute, as we do often on bills, it can be seen what would happen. My hon. friend talks about parliament reconsidering four hundred pieces of legislation such as the Canada Shipping Act-

maintopic: REVISED STATUTES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMMISSION TO EFFECT REVISION
speechtext: The changes in them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REVISED STATUTES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMMISSION TO EFFECT REVISION
speechtext:
-the Income War Tax Act, and many other acts, to see whether the commissioners have done their job properly. If that is done it would delay the revision of the statutes for years. I know enough about attendance at committees and the possibility
Revised Statutes of Canada

of getting members out of the house into committees, to say that if my hon. friend's suggestion were followed, the work would fall back on departmental officials, and those officials would be given the assurance that if there were no change in the law the statute would be accepted by the house. That is what would happen if my hon. friend's suggestions were accepted.
I would rather drop the revision of the statutes than embark upon something which will take five or ten years to accomplish, just because theoretically the house feels that it is unsafe to leave the work to a responsible commission, if the job is to be done faithfully and well.
I do not know why we should institute that new system at this time. It makes a good talking point, of course. But I ask hon. members to have some regard for the practical elements in the situation.

maintopic: REVISED STATUTES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMMISSION TO EFFECT REVISION
speechtext: I hope I am as practical a man as the minister. Having in mind the practical side of the matter. I am asking why this cannot be done. The last time this work took three and a half years. It is a greater work now than it was then?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REVISED STATUTES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMMISSION TO EFFECT REVISION
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: REVISED STATUTES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMMISSION TO EFFECT REVISION
speechtext:
Perhaps this time it will take more than three or four years. Why cannot the commissioners, as they complete their work of revision and consolidation of the statutes, pass it forward to parliament, session by session, within that period of time? Parliament could then review completely, through committees set up for the purpose, any changes that were proposed.
I do not for one moment suggest that parliament would carry out a revision, section by section, of 400 odd statutes which would come before us in four or five volumes. But surely parliament is going to accept its responsibility in connection with changes. The commission is not only authorized but is directed to make changes in certain ways. Who is to say in advance whether the commission will adhere to or confine themselves within the narrow interpretation of the instructions respecting changes? It is in the matter of changes made that I think parliament at this stage, in 1948, must take its stand. No matter what the commissioners may bring in, or put in the roll, when it comes here it becomes the law, without the slightest revision by parliament.
I have not so completely lost faith in parliament and the ability of parliament to do its legislative task with efficiency and expedition that I am prepared to accept the principle that parliament should not have any part in

the work of revision, or that parliament will be clogging its work if it insists upon review-ng the changes. Parliament has a task to do, and, regardless of what was done in the past, we have a situation to face today in 1948. Parliament has no business to turn its back on its duty.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: REVISED STATUTES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMMISSION TO EFFECT REVISION
speechtext: What about the criminal code?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REVISED STATUTES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMMISSION TO EFFECT REVISION
speechtext: The criminal code will have to be dealt with by some body other than this. Important changes should be made in it. Initially, revision of the criminal code is a departmental responsibility. Just as the revision and consolidation of the Income War Tax Act is the initial responsibility of the Department of Finance and the Department of National Revenue, in the same way, the revision and consolidation of the criminal code is the responsibility of the Department of Justice. For the purpose, the Department of Justice will have to secure the necessary appropriation and employ the best possible help to give advice. Then it will have to take the responsibility for changes in that law, just as it has in the past. The department will have to make recommendations to council, and council will make recommendations to the house. That is the only way in which we can deal with the criminal code. It is a different operation entirely from a consolidation of the statutes.

maintopic: REVISED STATUTES

speechtext:
Under the British constitution the courts are subservient to the legislatures, and those courts include not only the judges but all1 the crown officers. In the present procedure the government is simply wiping out the power of the legislature, and it is giving to judicial bodies, including crown officers, the power to pass those statutes over the head of parliament. And note that every bill tve pass gives crown officers the right to make rules and regulations thereunder which have the force of statute law. If that is law

Revised Statutes oj Canada
reform in this country, well then, I will say to the government that it is violating one of the most important principles in our constitution, namely that the courts are subservient to the legislatures.

speechtext: Let me call the hon, member's attention to the fact that this course was followed' in the two last revisions of 1906 and 1927. There may have been revisions before that, but the course of procedure being followed here was followed in the last two revisions.^

speechtext:
I should like to bring up a matter which has not been dealt with previously-the volume of orders in council that are not found in these statutes, but which amend, suspend or abrogate, in whole or in part, statutes passed by parliament. I first brought up this matter in 1942 by way of a question, when I asked for a list of statutes which had been amended, suspended or abrogated. The attitude taken' was that that was a question which just would not be answered because it had not occurred. Finally I placed a question on the order paper, it was passed as an order for return, and a list of statutes which had been suspended or amended or abrogated was brought down.
There are quite a few statutes in that position today. One statute was suspended in its operation even without an order in council. That was the one passed two years ago under which the railway companies were required, by a certain date, to abdicate any function in the matter of air transport. That date has long since passed, and the statute was not in fact suspended by an order in council or otherwise. A direction was simply made by the minister of reconstruction.
Section 4 of the bill reads:
There shall be appended to the said roll a schedule A similar in form to schedule A appended to the Revised Statutes of Canada of 1927; and the commission may include in the said schedule all acts and parts of acts which, though not expressly repealed, are superseded by the acts so consolidated, or are inconsistent therewith, and all acts and parts of acts which were for a temporary purpose, the force of which is spent.
As long as statutes are being suspended or abrogated in whole or in part by order in council-this is an occurrence not unusual under the Customs Tariff Act.-I think something should be done to provide a list of statutes or sections of statutes that are in a state of suspension or whose provisions are not
in effect. Today it is impossible for any person in the practice of law to know what the law is on any subject unless he has before him the various orders in council which have been passed and are still in effect.
I pass this on to the minister by way of suggestion. The passing of orders in council at an accelerated rate in the last ten years requires that something be done in order for the convenience of those charged with interpreting the law on behalf of clients and so that the judiciary may have before them at any one time the situation with respect to every statute. Would the minister be prepared to amend section 4 or add another section so that that certainty would be assured which is necessary if counsel are to advise? There should be a list of orders in council which detract or subtract from the effects of statutes in the appendix.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REVISED STATUTES
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMMISSION TO EFFECT REVISION
speechtext: A great deal of consideration would have to be given to that suggestion. I am under the impression that the repealing or amending of sections of acts by order in council was done under the War Measures Act, or the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, or the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act. That act expires on March 31 next, at which time these orders in council will lapse and lose their force. Unless there were some statutory amendment or repeal of the various sections, those sections would be there as the law.

May I suggest that the minister give consideration also to the question of revising, not only the orders in council but the regulations? Several years ago a useful act, the Regulations Act, was brought into effect in Ontario, under which all regulations issued by the provincial government were reviewed, brought up to date, classified and reissued. It had the effect of eliminating a lot of dead wood and making the present regulations known. There is a much larger body of federal orders in council. Such a measure applying both to orders in council and to regulations would be a most useful measure to put into effect here. I cannot speak too highly of the results obtained in Ontario from that statute. Under it the registrar of regulations is a continuing officer charged with the work of revision. New regulations must be submitted to him, and they are filed in public through him. I urge the minister to give consideration to that. Perhaps it is not as important as the revised statutes; nevertheless it is of great importance.

The commission in consolidating the said statutes, and in incorporating therewith the acts or parts of acts passed subsequent thereto and selected for inclusion therein as above provided, may make such alterations in their language as are requisite in order to preserve a uniform mode of expression, and may make such minor amendments as are necessary to bring out more clearly what they deem to be the intention of parliament or to reconcile seemingly inconsistent enactments or to correct clerical or typographical errors.

speechtext: Before the motion is put, I would suggest to the minister that he include the words which are in the Ontario act as to the consolidation of statutes, and which follow almost exactly what he has read, with a few minor changes. They have added this sentence: "And may include in such consolidation and revision such private acts". They relate to professions and callings. I would suggest that such private acts as are of general application throughout the province should be included. There are a great many private acts which affect a large number of people. As it is now, you require a whole library of the statutes of Canada in order to find them, because some of them go back a few years. Without this revision, you would have to obtain the statutes of thirty or forty years ago. There are some important acts which are called private acts and which affect a large percentage of the people of Canada. It would be a great convenience to solicitors and to the public if they were included.

This service supplies medical advice to the immigration branch of the Department of Mines and Resources, with regard to medical inspection of prospective immigrants, both abroad and at Canadian ports of entry. The medical examination is designed to assist the administrative immigration officers in prohibiting the entry of persons who are physically or mentally unfit, who might be a danger to the public health, or who probably would be unable to support themselves and would become a charge on the public. This is in accordance with the medical clauses of the Immigration Act and the regulations made pursuant thereto. This service also provides medical treatment for those individuals in immigration detention, under the authority of the Immigration Act and the regulations made pursuant thereto. It maintains and equips hospital accommodation for these purposes. It convenes medical boards of reference when needed. It pays costs of sending medical officers and their families overseas to conduct medical examinations in the countries of origin, wherever full-time officers or agencies are established. It pays the actual living expenses of those medical officers.
I may say that the present system of examination is much more complete than it ever was. X-rays are now required in the case of all immigrants. That is an improvement over the previous medical system and arises out of the experience the department has had during the past two years.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: This division, under the supervision of one of the outstanding nutritionists in the country, carries on much of its work through surveys which it makes at the request of provincial and other bodies, usually on recommendations made by the dominion council of health. I may say that the work of this division this past year has perhaps been more significant than in any other period. One important function is to carry on research on the state of nutrition of Canadians. It is a specialized service available to provincial health officers and others who find the nutritional information useful to them. Surveys have been made of the health of the populace in order that we may have more effective control and a more effective policy in improving and maintaining the health of Canadians. Surveys of this kind have been made in the maritime provinces, Quebec, Ontario and the prairie provinces, and requests are always on the desk of the nutritional director asking for further surveys. The work is both active and consultative. It is one of those branches of the service which I think is making a valuable contribution to our national life.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the minister make a statement on the whole subject of venereal disease and on what progress, if any, has been made within the limits of the department's jurisdiction in dealing with it? The department is assisting the provinces not only with certain grants under item 260 but also in connection with the distribution of drugs under item 261. What headway is being made in combating this scourge? There was a dominion-provincial conference of the officers of this department with those of provincial health departments, and I think useful results flowed from that conference. A program was also undertaken in connection with this disease in Alberta. Would the minister give us a statement as to the work that has been carried on during the past year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
As my hon. friend will realize, the new national health program involves a substantial increase in the activities of this division through the financial arrangements that are to be made and those already in effect now with the provinces. During the past year there has been a continued administration and distribution of the federal cash grant, materials and anti-venereal disease drugs to the provinces, according to the regulations set forth in order in council P.C. 1690. We have had the addition of a medical consultant, Doctor A. G. Laroche, to the staff of the federal division of venereal disease control. There has been the further development and distribution of venereal disease educational
material and other educational activities. For instance, there has been the continuation of projects involving the review of venereal disease documents of all service personnel and the provision of information upon request to provincial venereal disease control divisions. Arrangements have been undertaken for production of an additional supply of antiarsenical compound "BAL" for therapeutic and research purposes. We are engaged in preparing for the convening of the third federal-provincial conference of venereal disease control directors and participation in eastern and western regional conferences. There has been a continued compilation and expansion of quarterly statistical reports on venereal disease in Canada. Amendments have been enacted to sections of the criminal code dealing with prostitution. There has been increasing activity with respect to closer liaison with foreign countries and world health organizations. That, of course, is one of the important objectives in the control of venereal disease throughout the world.
The encouraging trend in the over-all venereal disease picture noted throughout the previous year has continued into the first quarter of 1948, as can. be demonstrated by a review of the number of reported cases of syphilis and gonorrhoea. There were 736 less cases of venereal disease, all types, reported by physicians and to provincial health departments during this period, representing an improvement of about nine per cent. Distributed between syphilis and gonorrhoea cases in numbers of 164 and 528 respectively permit me to say that these represent a six per cent improvement in syphilis	infections and
10 per cent in gonorrhoea cases. Early syphilis cases reported decreased by 213, or 24 per cent, while "syphilis others" increased by sixty-seven cases, or about four per cent.
It is both interesting and reassuring to note the precipitous fall in the reported cases of other types of venereal disease, namely forty-four cases, which, even though relatively insignificant in comparison with syphilis and gonorrhoea, represent an 80 per cent improvement.
I think my hon. friend will agree with me that, in spite of the serious proportions that still exist, much has been done in this field.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
From what my hon. friend said the other night, I fully expected him to ask this perfectly proper question. Because of the importance of the matter, perhaps I should deal with it in a somewhat more extended fashion than I otherwise would.
First of all, the expenditures are $6,652.61, and the unliquidated commitments are $28.27, or a total commitment of $6,680.88. May I say at the outset what I said last year, that this particular division of the department is so important that I as minister was not going to recommend the appointment of anyone who, in my judgment, had neither the competence nor the conviction in terms of belief in the general proposals of some form of system of health insurance.
I am sure the hon. member and the committee generally will agree with this. Certainly all one has to do is to speak to any minister who has had anything to do with the administration of this department to find out that the personnel in the country available for this work is extremely limited.
I am hoping to be able to announce shortly the name of an individual in this country whose eminence in the field of national health administration is unquestioned. It is hoped that that person will be able to take over the administration of this division of the department. I am sure that if satisfactory arrangements can be made in connection with getting this individual it will win not only the commendation of the house, but of the country.
The cut in the expenditures as indicated in the estimates is not at all indicative of the work that has gone on in this branch. I have arranged, during the past year, to have attached to this particular division Doctor B. D. B. Layton, who has been engaged in other pursuits in the department, and who had special qualifications for this work of health insurance studies. He has been engaged throughout the whole of the past year in this particular field. His salary is being voted in another division. So that, while the salary of the director under this particular branch has not been actually expended, the important thing is to make sure that the work is being done.

A. Ansley, the assistant director of health services, and Doctor Couture of the child and maternal health division, as well as Doctor Davidson, deputy minister of welfare, and Doctor Cameron, deputy minister of national health, have made invaluable contributions.

I have calculated by mental arithmetic that, during the past year, the value of the time that all these individuals have devoted to this particular division would have exceeded $100,000. While I cannot say what the supplementary estimates will reveal in this connection, my hon. friend will see there submissions for the administration of our new health program which I know will please him and satisfy most hon. members.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: I think the minister will recognize the spirit and the truth of what I say when I suggest that he might well withdraw the objections he made the other night when I mentioned this on the first item, because it has given him an opportunity to get ready the statement he has just made.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Although the minister has done some mental arithmetic to suggest that more than 8100,000 has been spent on this work, I do not think it can be taken that the people the minister talks about as being in other divisions spent their full time in two or three different capacities. The minister speaks of the great importance of this work and the considerable time or full time spent upon it by these various people, and yet they all have other jobs to do as well. As I listened to the minister's statement, I am afraid that it did not impress me as much as the words in it might be calculated to do.
The minister spoke of, and we agree with him, the desirability .of delaying any appointments in this branch until it is possible to get someone who would go into it with conviction. He says he wants somebody who really believes in a program of health insurance. Some of us are wondering whether or not the government has any conviction on this matter and really means to go ahead with it. There is not a great deal of difference between what the minister said today and what he said a year ago in reply to my deskmate, the hon. member for Mackenzie. As I listened to the names of the persons which he read they seemed to be in the main the same persons. I have not the figures before me that he gave us last year, but the minister has now told us that for the year 1947-48 there was appropriated $27,863, of which only $6,680.88 has been spent. I am afraid we shall have to judge the seriousness with which this problem has been pursued, by those figures.
I hope that the minister will not start this fall to prepare a similar statement with which to answer the same kind of question next year, but that rather in the meantime this important question will be pressed with real conviction. It is not good enough to be talking about what we are going to do in the future about the health of the Canadian people; it is
Supply-Health and Welfare

not good enough to be thinking about some glorious day in the distant future when people will no longer have to mortgage their whole lives in order to pay hospital, doctor and other bills; it is time for action now. I hope that the word "conviction" which the minister used is something that will be demonstrated by the pursuit of this important matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I cannot urge my hon. friend to accept what I have said if he does not want to, but I simply say there has never been as much activity in this division as there has been during the past year. The immensity of the program which we shall discuss next week clearly indicates the importance of that. If my hon. friend does not accept my word, I ask him to accept the word of Doctor Mott, who will confirm everything that I have said. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I should like to make some observations, but in view of the minis-ster's statement and the stress that he has placed upon the announcements to be made next week on the supplementary estimates, I am prepared to defer judgment on the work that has been done in this branch during the past year until we have the facts before us.
I simply say in passing that while the minister has been at pains to indicate the amount of work that has been done, and the fact that the actual amount of expense does not represent

the entire amount of work that has been devoted to this subject, nevertheless the committee will want some further proof of progress toward health insurance than he has yet given. I notice that under this item extensive studies are being made of health insurance, and I would suggest to the minister another form of insurance which I think should be established. I am thinking of insurance against improper diagnosis, where mistakes are made, by the medical profession. This matter came to my attention through a case with which I am familiar and which I regard as most serious. I do not suppose the suggestion I am about to make will be acceptable to the medical profession, for whom I have the highest regard. I say we have the highest regard for them because, if it were not for our medical practitioners, it would go hard with us. If we have a stomach ache the first thing we do is to call in a doctor and we have to trust him to prescribe for us.
I make no complaints, because I recognize that mistakes are sometimes made. Not even medical practitioners are perfect. We know, however, that when such mistakes are made the one who suffers is the patient and he has no redress. The medical man may say: Yes, he can sue through the courts. I think, however, it will be generally agreed that the patient has not one chance in a thousand of getting any redress by that procedure.

I suggest to the minister that something be done to set up an insurance scheme of this kind for the protection, not only of the patient but of the medical men themselves. The case in which I am particularly interested is this. A man took treatment for a certain malady which he thought was rheumatism, and the treatment given him consisted of radium, by which evidently he was burned. He is quite confident that in the process of the treatment a mistake was made. He sought legal advice, and the lawyer said to him, "I think we have a clear case. There is no question according to the story you have told me that a mistake was made; but I would not advise you to sue, because I do not believe you have one chance in a thousand of succeeding. You would have to call other medical practitioners to give advice". The lawyer then outlined the procedure that would have to be followed.
That man has been on his back for nearly a year. I visited him lately and he asked me whether something could not be done. It is costing him neatly $1,000 a month. While I was visiting him, the nurse dressed his wounds. ,In his back there is a hole six inches in diameter and one can see his bare spine. The medical men are doing all they can for him; and I thought, by the look of the wound, it was being gradually cleaned and eventually the doctors might be able to operate and bring the flesh over. Specialists were called in from the Department of Veterans Affairs, men who had been practising for many years in the treatment of wounded veterans. I believe they are doing a good job in the effort to make this man well, but unfortunately he is suffering. Some mistake was made, and he is left a sufferer who is heavily in debt.
These cases may not be numerous, but something should be done for the protection of both patients and practitioners. Perhaps the medical men will oppose a suggestion of this kind. I am not proposing that the patient pay the insurance. I am suggesting that the medical profession should have some type of insurance to protect them in such cases where patients must seek redress for mistakes that have been made.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: This is an important matter and it is one to which I have given a good deal of personal attention. I spent all last fall seeing for myself just what the situation was in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, the northern part of Ontario, some sections of Quebec along the St. Lawrence, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. I covered as many of the areas coming under this department as I could, and I am happy to be able to say there has been a reduction this year in the mortality rate among the Indians to the extent of seventeen per cent.
