Over the past year. It is due to many factors. It is due in part to improved nutritional knowledge and the dissemination of that knowledge among the Indian and Eskimo population. It is in large part due to the aggressive work that is being carried on in trying to bring the doctor and the nurse and the hospital into the more remote parts of our country.
Hon. gentlemen who live in Alberta, for instance, will bear testimony to the great value of the tuberculosis hospital, the Charles Cam-sell hospital, of 350 beds. It is one of the outstanding institutions of its kind devoted exclusively to the treatment of tuberculosis among the Indians. We have also had a hospital constructed at Coqualeetza, and a new hospital at Nanaimo, of 250 beds, as the hon. member for Nanaimo will likely confirm. I think he has visited the hospital. We have also another hospital at New Westminster; a new hospital at Brandon, another at The Pas, and we have a projected new hospital in one of the most densely populated Indian districts in Canada, the James bay district, where the tuberculosis rate is the highest.
The budget for health of Indians this year amounts to $7,500,000, as compared with 85,000,000 last year, and less than $700,000 in 1928. That gives one an idea of the accelerated program that is under way. Money is no measurement of these things, but it is an indication. That we have a real problem is emphasized by the fact that one per cent of the population of this country is responsible for twelve per cent of the tuberculosis in Canada among our native population. That is a challenge, and it is one which I am proud to say we are meeting on an accelerated plane.
There is a great deal yet to be done. I can say only this, that we have had the collaboration of many agencies. For instance, we are now in process of completing X-ray surveys of the Indian population in many parts of our country. I might mention the successful X-ray

survey made recently by our own director of Indian health services along with Doctor Tisdall of the Toronto sick children's hospital and others associated with them. That was a survey made in connection with anthropologists who are still in the area living among the Indians. This survey is giving to medical doctors and those who have to deal with the medical health of the Indian population a greater degree of knowledge and an ability to deal with the problem which has never existed before.
I should like to thank the medical profession throughout the country, and particularly some of the medical colleges, for what they have done and the assistance they have rendered the department in this important work. I should not like to single out any individuals, but I would take occasion to thank Doctor Trappier of Montreal, and his colleagues, for the highly important work they have done with regard to B.C.G., and the effect it has had on all our institutions, particularly the one under Doctor Simes at Fort Qu'Appelle in the Qu'Appelle valley.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I wish, first, to thank the minister for the full answer he has given to my question. Is there any change in the number of cases of tuberculosis among the Indians which are being reported? By treatment we can extend the life of tubercular patients, perhaps effect quite a number of cures. But the real control of tuberculosis lies in a better living standard and a better standard of hygiene in the homes. What is being done in that regard? Is the number of cases going up or coming down? I could understand that, because of the detection service in the department, the number might go up.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
As I said a moment ago, we have pursued a new policy of case finding through extensive X-ray surveys. The result of that improved method of detection has been a knowledge of a greater number of cases.
With regard to the social aspects of the problem, my reply would be that this matter is under the Department of Mines and Resources. However, what the hon. member says is quite true. Much of the condition we have been discussing is due to social conditions which are related to better nutrition and like factors. Until the problem is tackled in that basic way, it will always be a problem.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I was somewhat disappointed when, in the minister's report regarding tuberculosis among the Indians, he failed to give credit where credit belongs. Travelling from one reserve to another, evidently he did not visit the reserve at Golden Lake in the constituency of Renfrew North.

Supply-Health and Welfare
I hope the minister knows that what has been happening in the last few years on that reserve has had much to do with the reduction of tuberculosis among Indians all across Canada. I told the story in the house either last session or the session before; perhaps it was three years ago. A marvellous transformation has taken place at Golden Lake. Formerly it was considered one of the most unsatisfactory reserves in Canada. It is not a large one. Back about 1938 someone had the idea-
I had something to do with it myself-of making a definite change in the handling of that reserve. I remember suggesting that, by the purchase of a tractor so that the land could be torn up, thereby permitting the people to work, much could be done to permit the Indians to support themselves. Instead of a tractor being purchased, a good team of horses was bought. Fortunately a teamster who was proud of his horses and was anxious to keep them well groomed and harnessed was retained. Adequate machinery was purchased, and the Indians began working together. They dug a pit in which to keep their vegetables, and then began to grow vegetables.
The point I intended to develop was that it was in this reserve that the raising of goats was initiated. This was not done because of any shortage of milk. I doubt if many of these people drank goat's milk, because they had easy access to pasteurized milk at Egan-ville dairy. However, they raised these goats for shipment to other reserves. An Indian chief went to the Golden Lake camp from one of the Nova Scotia reserves, and took quite a number of the goats back with him. They are shipped throughout Canada, and even to the nomadic tribes in which Indian children never see milk from the time they are weaned.
These people when they are starting out in the spring in their canoes or boats, take their goat along. The goat's legs are tied and she goes along in the canoe. Thus they always have a supply of milk.
Then, let me point out that they have not had a new case of tuberculosis on Golden Lake reserve since they started keeping goats. In addition to raising their own vegetables, they raise pigs. Each Indian family is supplied with one or two pigs, as required. They also export chickens. They bring in the baby chicks in the spring of the year. When they are old enough to stand the trip they are shipped to far away reserves. Wonderful progress has been made in co-operative effort in that little community. In days gone by you would never see anything but a few green poles for fuel in front of their homes, but now they go out together on the reserve to cut their wood, which is sawn co-operatively. Now you see
in front of the Indian homes piles of dry wood to which they have access during the year.
They are constantly improving their homes and building more modern homes. A lot of credit is due to the efforts of the officials of the department and some fine people on the reserve. A celebration is to be held soon, and I should like to have the minister come and take a look around Golden Lake reserve. I am sure that many members who have been spending time in the Indian affairs committee could usefully spend some time in going to see what has been accomplished at Golden Lake.
Then a word in connection with these goats. As is known, these animals are hard to fence in, but this is being done. I understand that goat's milk plays a great part in the control of tuberculosis among Indians and, I presume, among white people as well.

There is another matter which I presume comes under this department. As is well known, Indian affairs are still under the Department of Mines and Resources, but the medical services are now provided by the Department of National Health and Welfare. I am wondering if the department has considered the granting of old age pensions to Indians. This will be a recommendation of the committee. I realize that this might not be on the same set-up as would apply to other citizens, because there is a provincial contribution along with the federal contribution; but from my own observations I know this would be greatly appreciated by the other Indians, the disabled Indians and the blind Indians. They need something to improve their security.
It has been my privilege 'to visit many Indian reserves. While some progress has been made, there is still room for improvement, because many of them are in a deplorable state. Credit should be given to the department for the health and. welfare work they have carried on. They have provided considerable medical facilities and care for the Indians; and I hope that this, along with the additional educational facilities that have been provided, will greatly improve their status.

speechtext:
I notice there is a reduction of $164,320 in this item. I presume that this reduction is due largely to the fact that new Indian hospitals have been established, as the minister intimated before the dinner recess, at such places as Nanaimo in my constituency. But there are also a large number of Indians who are not able to take advantage of these Indian hospitals which have been established in various localities. These other Indians have to go to the hospitals which are nearest to their reserves. It is known that the costs of running small hospitals have increased greatly in the last year or two. In fact, certain hospitals in my constituency, the King's Daughters' hospital at Duncan, and the Che-mainus general hospital, have found that they

Supply-Health and Welfare
are quite incapable of taking in the Indian patients at the rates at which they admitted them prior to this year. Would it be possible for grants to be made to these smaller hospitals which must admit the Indian patients, and which cannot afford to admit them under the contract prices which were arranged previously -between the Department of Indian Affairs, now the Indian health branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare? I should like to read an extract from a letter which I received recently from the administrator of the King's Daughters' hospital at Duncan which, I think, shows the difficulties under which these small hospitals are working. I shall read only the -pertinent paragraphs. I shall keep my remarks as brief as possible:
Our last year's financial statement showed a loss on operations of $1,429.74, and that in spite of the fact that we had received over $6,0-00 in donations from the public. The board of directors therefore decided that, if Indian patients want the services of the hospital, those services must be paid for at the regular hospital rates. You can understand then that if the Department of National Health and Welfare, Indian health services, will only pay a portion of the cost of hospitalization we must collect the difference from the Indian patients themselves. The hospital authorities have no wish or desire to bar the Indians from the hospital and its services, but the refusal of the Department of National Health and Welfare, Indian health services, to meet the increased cost of hospitalization has compelled them to adopt some measures to avoid loss on the hospitalization of Indian patients.
In consequence the board of directors have advised the Department of National Health and Welfare, Indian health services that, unless they agree to pay the increased costs as from March 1 last, as advised by us in a previous letter, we shall have no recourse but to refuse the admittance of Indian patients to the hospital, except in those cases where the Indian patient himself or herself deposits sufficient moneys with the hospital on entry for treatment to meet any additional cost over the $5.
That is the contract price. Another part of the letter goes on to say that the hospital authorities will, of course, admit Indian patients in case of emergency. I have another letter which points out:
Also we receive provincial and municipal grants in addition to this rate but for Indian patients neither of these grants are received.
In view of the fact that there is an item in the estimates which includes grants to hospitals which serve Indian patients, will the minister inform me what hospital receives these grants, and whether the Indians who are patients at the hospitals to which I have referred, namely, the King's Daughters' hospital at Duncan, and the Chemainus general hospital, receive grants? What steps
are being taken to ensure that the hospital fees which are necessary for these hospitals to ask, because of the increased cost of hospitalization, are being paid? Is it the policy of the department to allow Indians to go to the hospitals when these Indians themselves will be expected to pay a portion of their hospitalization?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The reason for the reduction in this item is that we gave a grant of $200,000 to the Fort William sanitorium on condition that they build a wing for the exclusive use of Indian patients. We have to consider our budgetary situation and our arrangement with other hospitals, apart from those which are departmentally owned and operated, such as the ones at Nanaimo and at Coqualeetza. We have a per diem rate arrangement with all other hospitals. I can appreciate the situation my hon. friend has outlined. It was, however, our belief, after careful consideration, that the fairest all-round method is the per diem rate arrangement, whereby a hospital taking care of an individual Indian is paid by the department for his hospitalization. That is the arrangement all through the country, not only in the particular case to which my hon. friend has referred, but throughout the dominion, apart from our own institutions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I wish to mention something that I brought to the attention of the minister, the department and the committee last year. There is a class of people who are sick, crippled or incapacitated in some way. With all the money that is being spent on national health and welfare, this class is entirely neglected. In my own constituency I have a number of cases about which I have written to the department from time to time but never could get anywhere with regard to my representations, because they would always refer me back to the welfare branch in the province, who in turn would not take care of these patients either. It is cases of that class that I wish to mention.
One case is that of a young man who is now thirty-five years of age, and who was crippled as a result of an accident when he was a child. He has been a burden, not only to himself but also to his parents who were not in a position to give him all the care and attention he should have had. After he lost his parents, who had taken care of him until that time, he became a burden on one of his brothers. This brother had a large family of his own, was engaged in fishing, and did 5849-339i
not have too much of this world's goods with which to take care of his crippled brother. When this young man was about thirty years of age the doctors decided that they might be able to do something for him by amputating one of his limbs. This they did, and he is now more of a cripple than ever. If it were not for the goodness of his own brother he would be thrown out of the world entirely alone. There should be something in national health and welfare to take care of cases of this kind. There are many of them across Canada.
Another case that I wish to bring to the attention of the committee and the minister is that of a lady about fifty years of age who, in an accident a few years ago, lost an arm and was hurt otherwise. She is nearly crippled and is incapable of doing any work. She is the wife of a labourer, and these people find it most difficult to get along.
In mentioning these two cases, I am mentioning only two out of the many there are throughout Canada. Why cannot something be done through the welfare branch by way of the allowances that are made, to take care of such cases? As a result of writing to the department, as I said in the beginning, all I receive is the answer that it does not come under their jurisdiction and that there is no vote for it. It stops at that. I thought that possibly, by my now bringing the matter before the minister, something could be done. Besides the items that are mentioned we find there is an extra vote, or one might call it a blank cheque, of over $1,000,000. Surely somewhere in that estimate there might be a chance for these unfortunate people. I should like the minister to take this into consideration and see what can be done in such cases.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I had intended saying
something on this matter, because of the remarks made the other night by the hon. member for Temiscouata. I thought possibly others were proposing to say something on the subject. That is why I did not rise at once.
May I say, in the first place, I am sure that, when we listened to the hon. member for Temiscouata the other night, we were all impressed by the important contribution he made to this subject at the time. This is not the first time he has raised the matter in the house. He has obviously, because of
Supply-Health and Welfare

the survey which he has conducted in his own county, given this matter a great deal of attention. I am sure that I speak for all hon, members when I say we are grateful to the hon. member for the point of view expressed and for the way in which he expressed his views the other night. He expressed himself somewhat along the same lines as the hon. member for Queens tonight. To both these hon. members and others I wish to say that I greatly appreciate what they have had to say.
This matter is one that is receiving my personal attention. The committee may recall a conference that was held between officials of the department and representatives of an association in Canada that has been promoting the interests involved in this particular project. I feel that what the hon. member for Temis-couata said the other night is, in principle, incontestable. When we consider that we are giving assistance by way of social legislation to so many groups in this country, it is impossible for anyone to argue against this matter in principle; because all of us know of many cases of individuals who, because of disability, are unable to seek employment, and who, in the absence of private means, are unable to have a proper maintenance. That, in principle is an incontestable situation. I certainly believe that, in the development of programs, that kind of group will have to receive consideration.
Let me say this. The matter of looking after those who require assistance at the hands of the state is not one for the federal government only. In this country we are spending close to 8800 million a year on social welfare. Of that total, the federal government is spending 80 per cent. Those are the important figures. I do not want to put this question on the basis of cost, and I am not putting it on that basis. But I believe that, in trying to approach this problem in an orderly way, we must bear in mind the responsibility of properly constituted authority in this country, namely, the responsibility of the municipality, of the province and of the federal government.
Having said that much, I believe I should also say this. It should not be overlooked that a great number of those who are in the disability class-not by any means all but a great proportion of them-received assistance through family allowances, veterans legislation and unemployment insurance. I do not say all the groups receive that assistance, but there is a great body that does. I am satisfied that the proper basis ultimately on which to arrange this sort of thing is through a system of dis-

ability insurance. I recognize that there will be a great body who could not benefit by that kind of scheme, because they have not the wherewithal to make contributions to what I think will ultimately come about, a contributory scheme covering disability and invalidity. For those who could not share in such a scheme there will have to be assistance given by the state, whether it be in the right of the municipality or in the right of the province or in the right of the dominion.
All I can say at the moment is that I am seized of the importance of this problem. We are paying this year, the dominion and the provinces together, by way of old age pensions, $100 million. That is a tremendous increase in the outlay by federal and provincial authorities, and of that amount the federal government pays close to 75 per cent. We have lowered the age for the blind to receive assistance from forty to twenty-one. That covers a considerable group of those who are handicapped, although there is still a great body left out, including the kind of cases referred to by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken and the cases referred to by the hon. member for Temiscouata. I repeat that all I can say tonight is that I recognize the importance of this problem, and I should like to think that, before I leave this parliament, I shall be able to say to the house that, in conjunction with other governmental authorities in this country, we have made, in terms of actual program, further progress with regard to this great class of our population. I assure the committee of my very deep interest in this matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my remarks really apply to the next item, but I have to leave shortly for a meeting of the banking and commerce committee, and perhaps I might be allowed on this item to raise two questions in connection with the family allowance which I have been discussing with the department for some considerable time. First, however, as to the matter raised by the hon. member for Temiscouata and discussed by the minister, some pension scheme for incapacitated people is something which, as the minister suggested, will have to be worked out in conjunction with the provincial authorities. There is no doubt about the need. I should like to leave this thought with the minister, that the most pathetic person in any group in need of social security is the woman of fifty to sixty-five years of age.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Even up to seventy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Yes, but I am going to stop at fifty to sixty-five. There are thousands of women in that age group in this country who

Supply-Health and Welfare
have contributed families to the nation, who in turn went to war to save the institutions of this country. These women now find themselves with their families gone and themselves unable to work and with nowhere to turn for a livelihood. In each province there is a mothers' allowance act, but it is really a misnomer. It is not a mothers' allowance, because the children are the qualifying factor. Could not the minister, when he is working out with the provincial governments his comprehensive health program, suggest that they include women in that category under their mothers' allowance acts? In my own part of the country and elsewhere in Canada I run into hundreds of women who are in those circumstances, and they are the most pathetic group in society. They have nowhere to turn. Their families are gone; they have no income, and all they can do is wait for the old age pension. The minister would be doing a real service in provoking thought by the provincial governments on that subject.
What I rose to say was this. There are two sore spots in connection with the family allowance. First, there is the fact that children who remain in institutions in Canada cannot receive the family allowance. I have discussed this matter in the house and have had considerable correspondence about it with the previous minister, and it has been taken care of to some extent by the inclusion of children who were boarded out from such institutions. The allowance can be got through the children's aid society under those circumstances. But there is another considerable group who do not get the allowance. I know the minister is sympathetic. Would he not consider including children who remain in institutions for certain reasons? When we framed the act we understood that it was for the benefit of all children born in Canada, but here is one category that is not included.
Secondly, could the family allowance not be continued beyond the statutory age for children who are continuing their education? This should be given serious consideration. Many widows find themselves with a son or daughter on their hands who wants to continue his or her education and learn a profession, but the allowance is cut off at the age of sixteen. The department might very well continue the allowance for two or three years under those circumstances.
I conclude by saying this. I have had a great deal to do with the family allowance branch in Nova Scotia, and I think we who do a lot of criticizing should hand out a bouquet where it is deserved. I want to tell the minister that he has, administering his district branch in Nova Scotia, a wonderful personnel. They have done an excellent job
right from scratch, and the branch there, with the exception of the one or two points I have mentioned, over which the local personnel have no control, is running like a well-oiled machine. I know the minister will do what he can to iron out the few kinks that still remain in the act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I wish to say a few words on the question of social security. I have listened closely to what the minister had to say and, while what he said is undoubtedly true, I do not believe that it should be a bar to our working toward a social security program. I have, during the last few days when the minister's estimates were under discussion, heard several members bring to his attention some particular case of helplessness for which they wanted something done. These cases could be multiplied a hundredfold, and that would not include them all. So what is required in Canada is an over-all social security program which will provide for every person who is prevented from making a living for himself for reasons beyond his control. There is no way in which we can provide for people in a piecemeal way.
Then we come to the question of how this is to be paid for. It can be paid for by the contributions of people either by way of taxes or in other ways. When I hear people who are continually complaining about high taxes and who urge for more and better social services, and more of almost everything else, it leads me to believe that there is something wrong. There seems to be some lack of sincerity or lack of understanding.
Those of us who have most of the good things of life will have to share them with those who have not. There is no other way in which these people can be cared for. There is no magic wand we can wave and bring goods and services to people, without taking those goods and services from the people who created them. Under our present economic set-up, that is done by way of taxes. As the federal government is in the position where it has power to collect the largest amount of taxation, undoubtedly it will have to take the greatest responsibility for providing those services.
Today municipalities are overburdened. They cannot meet all the requirements made upon them. Most of the provinces are not in a much better position. Consequently the government that has the power to raise money must take the responsibility for providing those services, along with the responsibility of
Supply-Health and Welfare

making the necessary arrangements with other governments to meet their constitutional requirements.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I should like to say something about the statement made by the minister. I think all hon. members appreciate the minister's remark regarding the responsibility of the provinces and municipalities as well as that of the federal government. On the other hand, I am sure we all realize that in the past the federal government has apparently taken the attitude that it alone has the responsibility of taking care of the needs of people in foreign nations. That is to say, we have made large contributions to foreign nations. We have not said we could do it only on the understanding that contributions would be made by the provinces and the municipalities.
We as a federal body have assumed full responsibility for making those contributions, without tying the provinces and municipalities in as well. Therefore it seems to many people in this country that our own people should be considered just as favourably as people in foreign nations. Surely there can be no group in Canada who have a greater right to expect priority against the production of the country than those who are incapacitated and unable to take care of themselves. I cannot follow the minister's statement that this can be done only if the cost is borne by the provinces and the municipalities. As I have said, we have not hesitated to make these expenditures in connection with foreign nations. If we can help to restore better conditions in foreign countries, then surely we can afford to look after our own people without haggling over the responsibility of this or that province.
The minister has emphasized the fact that the federal government is already paying out large sums of money. I do not think that is an important point. The question is how far short that falls of meeting the requirements of those in Canada who are disabled. If we pay out a billion dollars, then how much more do we have to pay out in order to see that all those people who are physically incapacitated are cared for?
The other day I attended a dinner in which a gentleman named Doctor Graham, I believe, spoke about arthritis. I was struck by one statement he made. He said that certain people still come to him and ask him to diagnose their conditions and to prescribe what should be done. Then- he said, "Of what use would it be for me to prescribe that a person should rest, when that individual may be a mother with five children, and when
['Mr. Maelnnis,]
I know that as soon as she leaves me she will go home and look after those children? Is there any use in my prescribing rest when I know she cannot rest?"
This is not a question of the number of doctors or nurses we have or the hospital accommodation available. The need here is for some assistance to be given to people of that kind, so that they can take a rest or take the required treatment. That is something we must take into consideration.
I realize that this is not the opportune time to advocate the paying out of large sums of money for any body of people, because we are now in an inflationary period. And to the extent that inflation exists, I would not for one moment criticize the government for continuing to maintain fairly heavy taxation on the people in the high-income brackets. But that condition will not always obtain. Certainly it was not the case in the thirties, when production was at less than 50 per cent of capacity. It would not have beeen necessary at that time to maintain heavy taxation in order to make more wealth available to those people who were physically incapacitated.
The reason the federal government can assume this responsibility so much more easily than the provinces and the municipalities is that the federal government has access to moneys to which neither -the provinces nor the municipalities have access. The federal authorities have different means of raising money. Therefore I was glad to hear the minister say this is a problem which he realizes the federal government will have to consider, and to which no doubt it is giving consideration. I hope that by next year the minister will be able to bring down a comprehensive program to take care of, not just some of the people who are incapacitated, such as the blind, but all people in Canada who are physically disabled and cannot take care of themselves.

When the question of sending millions of dollars to Europe for the assistance of European children was placed before parliament, that money was sent quickly. It did not take long to do it, and it was a fine gesture. But if we cannot provide for our own people who are in an unfortunate condition, then surely there was some exaggeration in those expenditures.

have listened to a great deal of criticism which may be quite proper, but I think the minister has done exceedingly well for his first appearance. He has shown an appreciation of the problem and a determination to attack it, which is altogether commendable.
I should like to draw to his attention one important fact which may not be welcome, but which is something his government and his party must face. speechtext:
I have another matter to bring up in connection with the activities of the welfare branch. This branch gives out-information, and in some cases it should be given information. We hear a lot about beautifying Ottawa. Ottawa is like a woman with make-up on only half her face, beautiful on one side and ugly on the other. You have only to go to the eastern and western parts of the city and to some quarters in the immediate vicinity to find slums. Every time we come here we hear about the beautification of Ottawa.
Some years ago I had something to do with the old Department of National Health and Welfare. At the request of the judges of the supreme court I drew to the attention of the then minister the condition of the old supreme court building. An investigation was held and it was condemned as being unhealthy for the judges. One judge became very ill because of the drafts and overheating, and another judge died. He told me before he died that he was dying because of the nonsalubrious condition of the building. I am not exaggerating. My reward for denouncing the condition of that building was to receive from the minister an official copy of the investigation. That was my reward for telling the truth. My reward in this case will be the removal of these slums as the next step in beautifying the capital city of Ottawa.
I have another ease I want to cite to show the connection that exists between the department of health and some of the other departments. I should like to give the particulars of this very sad case which requires immediate welfare treatment. I will not give any names, because these people live in my constituency. This man is a good labourer. He worked for two weeks at night and then he worked during the day at a certain manufacturing plant. He worked eleven hours
Supply-Health and Welfare

during the day and thirteen hours at night.
When he was working at night he put in eighty hours a week.
In 1947 he bought a house which is now occupied by three persons, the father, the mother and a boy, twenty-five years of age. This man, whose case I am bringing up, has ten children, ranging in ages from eighteen to two years. They occupy a tourist cabin which measures eighteen feet by fourteen feet. They had to put three children in the orphanage. There are six who sleep in a room eight feet wide. The father, mother and baby are in one bed, while three of the daughters are in another. In the other small room are two boys sleeping in one bed, with a third one sleeping on two trunks.
The kitchen is ten by twelve feet. There is table, stove, washing machine, sewing machine, radio and three rocking chairs. Around the family table are eight chairs which cannot be moved. The toilet is close to the kitchen cupboard and the partition does not go to the ceiling. There is no door on it. There are only 320 cubic feet of air for nine persons, and the mother has been in the hospital for several months for a TIB. prevention cure.

May I ask the minister two questions with respect to family allowances? One of them is the question I asked the other night when we were on the general item. Has consideration been given to amending the act so as to make it possible for children to qualify for the allowance in less than the three years required at present? When I drew this matter to the attention of the minister the other night I stated that at that time I could not recall whether this point had been discussed when the act was passed in 1944. Since then, I have looked up the debate on the point, and I found that there was a fair amount of discussion on it. The Prime Minister stated that in his view it was a good idea to start off with that provision in it and to see how the matter worked.
We have now had a few years of administration of the act. I think the position taken the other night by the hon. member for Dauphin is valid, namely, that with children coming to Canada, children of immigrants from the United Kingdom and from other parts of the world, it seems unfair that they should have the disability of not getting the allowance as other children do in this country. After all, the purpose of the allowance is to make it possible for all children to have the best possible chance.
My second question relates to the amount of the allowance. In view of the increased cost of living-and the minister in his capacity as chairman of the prices committee knows all about it-has consideration been given to increasing the scale of the allowance? As the minister knows, the increased cost of living, particularly the increased cost of food, hits hardest at families in the lower income brackets, and families with a larger number of children. It does seem to me that this would be one way to help the people that need it. Can the minister answer my two questions?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
A number of questions on this matter of family allowances were put the other night, and I promised to deal with them all in one reply, including the two questions mentioned by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. On the first of July the family allowances program will be three years
Supply-Health and Welfare

. old. I believe the program has fully justified the hopes of those who shared the responsibility of placing it upon the statute books of our country. I think it is recognized universally as being the most comprehensive and generous family allowances act to be found anywhere. The benefits paid under the act are, by and large, more generous than those of any other system in existence at present. That the program has gained increased favour with the Canadian people is indicated, I think, by the Gallup polls which have been taken this year and in the two previous years of the act's existence. This shows a steady increase over the last three years in the numbers of our fellow countrymen who, as a result of their experiences with the family allowances program, have expressed themselves as being in favour of this key item in our social security program. The percentage of those favouring the program has now risen to 75 per cent of the total population. The percentage of those expressing themselves as opposed to family allowances has constantly dwindled and now is shown to be somewhere in the neighbourhood of a little less than eight per cent of our total population. Rarely does any public opinion poll show such an overwhelming majority of sentiment in favour, and such a relatively small percentage opposed to any given measure or proposal.
Since I put on Hansard the table asked for by the hon. member for Eglinton the other night, I have noticed that considerable attention has been paid in the press and elsewhere to these tables showing the increase in the total expenditures under family allowances during the years they have been in operation.
These tables showed that for the nine months of the fiscal year 1945-46 the total expenditures on family allowances amounted to 8172,632,146, or an average of a little over $19,000,000 a month. For the full fiscal year 1946-47, the expenditures totalled $245,140,000, or an average of a little less than $20,500,000 a month. The expenditures for the fiscal year just ended amount to $263,000,000, or an average of a little less than $22,500,000 a month; and the estimates for the current year -I ask the committee to bear these figures in mind-indicate that we shall require something in the neighbourhood of $267,000,000, or almost $22,500,000 a month.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: How do you account for that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I shall deal with that in a minute.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Is it
breeding?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
That would be one of the reasons. I shall come to the reasons in a moment. I call the attention of the committee to the fact that, since the act came into force, there has been distributed a total of $725,000,000 to approximately 3,750,000 children, representing over 1,650,000 families in our country.
The reasons for this progressive increase in expenditures are not difficult to understand. The experience of most countries has been that in the immediate post-war years there has been a very sharp increase in the birth rate. This is due, of course, to the fact that the post-war year's have seen a marked rise in the rate of marriages and in the rate of new family formations, as hundreds of thousands of men have returned from military service overseas to civilian life.
It should be noted incidentally that this increase in the marriage rate, and consequent increase in the birth rate, has no direct connection with family allowances as such. This can be shown by comparing the Canadian birth rate in the immediate post-war years with the United States birth rate. Despite the fact that family allowances are not provided in the social security program of the United States, the birth rate in that country during the post-war years has risen even more sharply than in Canada.
In our country, however, there has been during the last few years a most remarkable increase in the number of births. From 1937, the year in which the number of births sank to its lowest point of 220,000, there had been a slow increase until the year 1945 when births totalled some 288,000. The average increase for this eight-year period was something in the nature of 8,000 additional births a year. From 1945 to 1946 the total births jumped from 288,000 to 330,000, and from 1946 to 1947 they rose still further to a total of some 358,000 for the last calendar year.
In other words, total births have increased no less than 70,000, from 228,000 to 358,000 in the last two years. This increase is more than the total increase which took place in the preceding eight years. It is this unusually large post-war increase in the total number of births occurring annually in our country which has accounted in large part for the increase in the total annual expenditures for this program.
As will be noted from the estimates for the current fiscal year, it is not expected that the increase from 1947-48 to 1948-49 will be as great as it has been for the previous period. The total anticipated increase for the current fiscal year will be in the neighbourhood of $4,000,000. The figures appearing

Supply-Health and Welfare
currently from month to month show that the post-war situation regarding marriages and births is beginning to normalize itself, and it is expected that, as a result of this, the annual expenditure on family allowances will tend to increase less sharply in the course of the next few years and will ultimately flatten out at a level not markedly higher than the level which will prevail for the current fiscal year.
At the present time the provisions of the Family Allowances Act cover nearly all the children of Canada, It is probably safe to say that not more than 50,000 children in all Canada fail to benefit at the present time from the provisions of this legislation. One of the most significant groups in this 50,000 consists of children who are debarred from receiving immediately the benefits of the family allowance by the fact that they have come recently to Canada iwith their parents and have not yet established three years residence in this country as required by the legislation.
We have been giving serious consideration to this aspect of the problem, particularly in connection with our immigration policy. A substantial number of representations have been received from several organizations interested in the welfare of immigrants; and the department is at the present time engaged in the study of how best, adequately and fairly, in the light of all considerations, to meet this problem.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: May I interrupt the minister for a moment? I feel confident that if the question were put to a vote in the House of Commons the proposal would receive unanimous support, that all new children brought to this country under our immigration schemes should receive the same treatment as is given to every Canadian-born child in the way of benefits from family allowance, and that not more than a period of six months should elapse, and possibly not three months. This is a most serious matter. I have been receiving letters from people who have recently arrived in the country. We told them of the great benefits they would derive here; and we find that mothers of little children, under the present law, cannot receive the benefits that Canadian-born children receive, until a period of three years has elapsed. This is something that should be taken up at once. I do not think a period of more than six months should elapse before the child arriving in this country receives these benefits. They have come here to become Canadians for the future; and they should receive, almost immediately, the benefits that are given under this act. I believe the unanimous feeling of hon. members, representing all parts of 'Canada, irrespective of parties, would be in support of this suggestion.

This act has been in existence for only three years, and it is important that we do not start tinkering with it. Instead of doing good, it might do harm. We have good reason for conjectures as to what some of the abuses might be. This is the most generous act of its kind to be found anywhere; and people coming here, with no intention of remaining, because they are en route to the United States, would automatically get the benefit of the family allowance, if there were not in the act some provision regarding residence. There are considerations of this sort that one must bear in mind, and we are studying the matter carefully.
What I want to say about the family allowance administration is this. I greatly appreciate what was said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South in praising the administration, particularly in his part of Canada. As Minister of National Health and Welfare, I have had to authorize but eight prosecutions for fraudulent receipt of family allowances by individuals in this dominion. I think that is a great tribute to the people of this country. I am not saying that is the only extent of abuse. That would perhaps be placing an assessment on human nature that would be extravagant. But through the surveys that we conduct and through the special arrangements that we have had with the provinces, our judgment in the administration is that the attitude of the public toward this matter is an honourable one, and I believe that this is the place to say it.
I believe it is something of a record to be able to say that with respect to a matter involving over $725 million, going into almost one and three-quarter million homes, representing three and three-quarters of a million children, the minister responsible for the administration of the act has had to authorize but eight prosecutions. I feel that, from all the evidence that we can get, from the increase in the consumption of milk, in the use of medicines, cod liver oil and things like that,
Supply-Health and Welfare

family allowances have been a good thing. I have on my desk a report from the minister of education of Ontario, who is also premier of that province, pointing to the increase in the school attendance in Ontario since the introduction of family allowances. The same thing is true of every province. So, in making this abbreviated report on an important social welfare program, I think the house and the country may be well satisfied in the decision that was made when it was decided to establish family allowances in Canada.

The answer that is usually given is that it is not compulsory; but for income tax assessment purposes it is compulsory.
There should be a line of demarcation. If those who have incomes of $3,000 and over do not care to register their children to receive the family allowance they should not be required to do so, and the act should so provide. Two quite distinct matters are involved here. One is the matter of obtaining money by false pretences or in breach of the provisions of the Family Allowances Act, section 14, which deals with offences.

the first instance, are disbursed for the benefit of the family. The minister's statement has dealt with the first matter only. Earlier in the evening I started to say something about those people who have been unfortunate enough to lose their sight. I think everyone in the house would agree to doing whatever can be done to help these people. We should do as much as we possibly can for them. The Canadian National Institute for the Blind has put out a pamphlet, and I imagine that every hon. member has received a copy similar to the one I hold in my hand. They set out six points which they want to bring to the attention of the minister and which are as follows:
1.	The creation of a blind persons' act separate from and independent of the Old Age Pensions Act.
2.	The use of the term "'blindness allowance" and elimination of the term "pension."
3.	The elimination of the means test in the award of the blindness allowance.
4.	An adequate rate of blindness allowance in relation to the cost of living. Under present circumstances, this would appear to be not less than $40 per month, preferably uniform for all provinces.
5.	The reduction of the present residence requirement from twenty years to five years, in the case of a person with normal vision who has taken up residence in Canada in good faith and at any time thereafter has lost his sight.

Supply-Health and Welfare
6.	Adequate provision for medical or surgical treatment for eye conditions to conserve or to restore vision and to prevent blindness.
I referred to the sixth item earlier in the evening. Everything that can possibly be done should be done to prevent blindness. The medical profession has made sufficient progress to save the sight of many people. I could talk for a long time on this, but I think what I have said will impress the minister with the necessity of further work being done. With the support of the government and with a sympathetic public, I am sure we can make the wishes of those who have been deprived of sight come true.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I want briefly to support the views which the hon. member for Selkirk has expressed. I have no doubt that the requests which have been made here have captivated the entire sympathy of the minister and of all members of the House of Commons as well as of the people of Canada. This is something which has no place in politics. I imagine that, in pursuing the course which has been suggested, the only difficulty of the minister will be, first, the type of scheme to help these people and, second, the matter of money.
No one can think of a legitimate reason why the unfortunate blind in our country should be associated with old age pensions. One can think of being deaf; one can think of having an accident of some kind, but I know that I at any rate cannot comprehend my position if I were stricken blind. I am not sufficiently courageous, nor have I the imagination even to contemplate a disaster so great as that.
I realize that during the present session of parliament no new act could be passed, but in support of the hon. member for Selkirk we are asking this, and I am sure we shall receive the sympathetic consideration of the minister. I want also to speak to his colleagues. When we speak of social service, security and all those things we are agreed on one thing, that this country will subscribe sufficient money by way of taxation to take care of those persons who, through injury or through accident at birth or through other causes no fault of their own, are without sight. I am sure that the minister and this whole House of Commons will not think of being penurious when dealing with a matter of this kind.
Let us think of two men, eighteen to twenty years of age, one blind and the other with his sight. One cannot conceive of the handicap or cannot get into his head any idea of any fairness in competition in the labour markets of the world, and I use the word "labour" in its biggest and broadest
sense, to say nothing of the loss of sight itself. On the economic side one immediately appreciates the handicap of these persons. The most that any of us can do tonight so far as our legislation is concerned, because our legislative life in this session is, I hope, nearing an immediate end, is to suggest this separation. I can see no reason for applying the means test, except at a point where the blind person is earning sufficient money to live in even greater comfort than the ordinary person because of the tremendous handicap that he has in the loss of sight. Braille has been a great thing. It gives the blind person the pleasure of some reading.
With respect to the age limit, we did reduce it at the last session; but there is no reason why we should have taken the age of twenty or twenty-one years, whichever it is, or why we should not have said fifteen years or ten years. I am not suggesting for one moment that when blind people come to Canada this country should assume the burden for them, but I am saying that when persons come here with the intention of living here, making a stake here, helping us along with our business, and they are stricken with blindness, they should not have to wait the length of time prescribed in our present statute. After all, the amount of money is very far from terrific; it is really a reasonable sum. I heartily commend what was said by the hon. member for Selkirk, that if sufficient funds were in the hands of people who had oncoming blindness, and through that assistance they were permitted to go to an ophthalmologist-it is a great big word that I have difficulty with- to one of those persons who might arrest the progress of the disease, or in early years even restore complete sight, then could we go home and say truly we have done a job worthwhile for the people who have suffered more from that illness or from that disability than from any other disability of which I have any cognizance?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
There are many hon. members who will deplore the fact that we have practically reached the end of the session and we have seen on the order paper as yet no indication of any intention on the part of the government to introduce legislation with respect to old age pensions. I do not need to review the debate that was held in this chamber a year ago on the 1947 amendments to the Old Age Pensions Act; but I remind the committee that the increase at that time was quite inadequate to sustain health. It meant that the dominion, by setting the basic pension at only $30 a month, with 75 per cent contribution by the dominion to a maximum pension on that basis, was not
Supply-Health and Welfare

accepting the responsibility for the adequate maintenance of the old age pensioners, and was throwing the residual responsibility on the provinces where it does not belong.
When one has regard to the fact that the dominion has great resources at its disposal; that provincial boundaries have no place in meeting the needs of our aged pensioners, that certainly was a position which could not commend itself to the judgment of many of us in this chamber. The government did not go nearly far enough. The principle that the dominion was setting a limit to its responsibility was unsound.
This question is tied up, of course, with the larger question of the basic approach to the meeting of the needs of aged people. We call the present payment an old age pension. The word "pension" is perhaps a polite term to apply to the payment. It is not a pension at all in the strict and proper sense of the word. It is a payment without relation ait all to the question of right and title on the part of the recipient. There will be-surely it is apparent by now-no final solution of this problem until the whole question of a proper pension scheme, with retirement features, on a contributory basis, is taken up in this country, on the basis of joint action on the part of the dominion and the provinces. I have no doubt that all the provinces will be prepared to participate in any reasonable scheme if the dominion will take action and accept its responsibilities in this regard.
The minister is well acquainted with representations made to him and to the government on this subject by the Canadian welfare council, a body whose views on this and other welfare questions are entitled to the highest respect, as I am sure the minister will readily acknowledge. He will remember that the point on which the Canadian welfare council criticized the proposals of the dominion-provincial conferences of 1945 and 1946 was that they did not get at the root of this problem, and did not seek to bring about what will eventually be the only possible and comprehensive solution, namely, a contributory overall scheme that will provide adequate retirement, or old age, insurance for aged people of this country.
An interesting news report emanated from Ottawa in January last. I take it that there was some basis for the report which appeared in the press. It suggested that some plans were under way in the department at that time for drafting and submitting to parliament a contributory old age pensions scheme. It was suggested in this news article that a bill embodying such a scheme would be submitted

to parliament at the present session. A good many of us have been looking patiently for the introduction of such a measure. None has been indicated as yet. May I read briefly to the committee the substance of this report which appeared in the Globe and Mail on January 15? I shall refer to part of it. It says:
Measures covering a contributory _ old age pension scheme as well as a health insurance plan are being drafted, with a view to having both bills presented to the commons at the coming session. There has been no cabinet discussion of Health Minister Martin's new plans, and it is likely that they will come in for careful and lengthy scrutiny. It is the hope of the minister and the department, however, that both bills will be on the statute book before parliament prorogues at midsummer.
Both bits of legislation are based on extensive studies made in the department, using the original dominion-provincial proposals of August, 1945, as a starting point.
In both cases the legislation would follow the pattern of the original Old Age Pensions Act-

the necessity for a courageous approach to the

problem and for finding a solution of the kind that ultimately must be sought, a solution of the kind which the government has been asked on more than one occasion to bring in. At one stage of the session the air was filled with rumours that the government would bring in such a plan, and we are now on the eve of prorogation without such a plan, without any breath of intimation from the government that any such plan is to be brought in. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words in support of the plea made by the hon. member for Selkirk and the hon. member for Calgary West. I wish also to commend the minister, even at this late date, for the action he took last session in bringing down an amendment reducing the age from forty to twenty-one in the case of blind persons receiving pensions. That, I believe, received favourable comment throughout the dominion, and I do not think we have felt the loss that has resulted from that action.
In connection with old age pensions in general, I wish to ask a few questions. The first has reference to the prairie farm assistance bonus cheques received by old age pensioners. I should like to know just how these cheques are treated by the department, whether they are allowed as income or otherwise. Perhaps the minister is not aware that farmers have to contribute one per cent of their grain cheques to a fund known as the prairie farm assistance fund, and when the average crop goes below a certain number of bushels per acre the people
contributing receive a small payment on account of the low average yield. I understand that there is some conflict in respect of the treatment of this matter. I would ask the minister to give an explanation of the method used and the reason for its adoption. After that, there are two or three more questions I wish to ask.
(Mr. MARTIN: The Department of Justice has ruled that as income.

speechtext:
Thank you. The next question is in connection with proof of age. Recently I came across a number of cases, particularly affecting Ukrainians and Polish people, and other people from those countries who came here many years ago. Because of the spelling and pronunciation of their names, mistakes were made in recording them as they came here, with the result that, after they have spent the useful part of their lives here and have reached the age of seventy, they are unable to produce proof of age. I understand that many of them are denied pension on this account. In some cases I have tried every method I could think of and have been unable to get proof of age. I wonder what action has been taken by the department so far as these cases are concerned, or whether any method can be found whereby these people can be granted their pensions.

speechtext: I am aware that these people can go to the bureau of statistics or the old age pension branch in the province and try to get through the census records some proof of their age, but in some cases we have been unable to prove age. Other methods such as immigration records and filing on homesteads having failed, I suggest that some method should be found whereby these people can be enabled to get their pensions.

I wish to support once again the plea for the 'blind so well put forward by the hon. member for Selkirk and others who followed him tonight. I wish also to express my active interest in the old age pension question, not by making another speech tonight but by putting three questions to the minister.
My first question relates to the proposals made to the provinces by the dominion government in 1945, which included a $30 universal pension for all Canadians seventy years of age and over, without any means test, together with a means-test allowance for those between sixty-five and sixty-nine years of age. My question is this. Is the government considering implementing that proposal, at least in the case of provinces that have signed the taxation agreement?
My second question is one that arises particularly if the answer to the first question is either in the negative or a delayed reply. Is the government considering increasing the amount of $30, which is now in the basic Old Age Pensions Act, to a larger amount? I refer now not to pressure that may be put on the provinces to add to it. My direct question is this. Is the government considering an increase in the basic amount provided in the federal statute?
My third question relates to an over-all scheme, or more specifically, to tie it down to this field, to the question of contributory old age pensions. Is the government considering a contributory old age pension plan for presentation to parliament at an early date?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I wish to say a few words in support of the six-point program sponsored by the Canadian Council of the Blind and the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. I think it is unnecessary for me to mention those six points again. The minister is well aware of them, and, I believe he is favourably disposed toward them.
I wish to say one word in connection with point number four, which I believe is most important. That is the one with regard to the twenty-year residence law Which is now in force. It is most ridiculous that a person coming to Canada to live, with the intention of making Canada his home, if he should have difficulty, get into an accident or have some mishap whereby he loses his sight, must remain in this country for twenty years before he can get this pension. As I said, this is a most ridiculous situation. I hope the minister will

lend his support in favour of these six points.
I might say here I see that there is a $27,200,000 increase in this particular item. I wonder if any portion of that is to go toward increasing pensions for the blind?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I should now like to renew the question I asked earlier with respect to income tax. I believe this is a spot where I might expect the minister, when he gives an answer to many questions that have been asked, to tell the committee if the department have recognized the recommendation by the special committee on Indian affairs, and whether they will now be prepared to grant a pension in kind-an old age pension, as it is now called- to the aged Indians on the various reserves.
I should also like to take this opportunity to underline and support the views that have been expressed with respect to the blind. I wish to go one step farther. I think the blind suffer a terrible disability, but there are other types of disablement, both physical and mental. I believe this country can afford to assume the burden in order to release society of that responsibility-I refer particularly to the parents of children who are afflicted by mental disease or physical incapacity- so that when the children attain the age of twenty-one years the state should provide for those unfortunate victims of disablement, which is no fault of their own, but who remain a burden to those whose responsibility they are, whereas the nation could well afford to provide for them.
I should also like to express a view which has been expressed before by myself and others,' that I believe the means test should be removed as of age seventy, that the amount should be increased, and that the pension should be available at the age of sixty-five, subject to a means test if necessary, but certainly at age seventy. I could elaborate at considerable length on the reasons why I think that would be a good move and would tend to promote thrift; because those people, in anticipation of a pension, knowing it would be available for them upon proving their age,

Supply-Health and IVeljare
would probably continue to save their money and might not even need a pension. But as matters stand at the present time, very often between the age of sixty and seventy people dispose of their small estates in order that they may obtain a pension, and the country is the loser.
Once again I say it is unfortunate that we use that term "old age pension", because I feel it does not properly describe the objective. I think it would be far better if the title "retirement allowance" were used, since one of the objectives surely is to remove from the labour market those who have served their country and their community, who are entitled to some reward, and are encouraged by the very terms of the act to desire retirement with a greater sense of security than they have at the present time. The country could well afford to be more generous to those who are seventy years of age and over, without the means test, even though we continue to apply it in connection with any reduction of age that might be anticipated. But I am particularly asking the minister if the government have given consideration to granting a pension in kind for all aged Indians on the various reservations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
May I add my support to the hon. member for Grey North in advocating abolition of the means test for all blind people, abolition of the means test for all old age pensioners at the present time and certainly after they have reached the age of seventy; also that great consideration be given to the unfortunate children in this country who find themselves crippled through one means or another, and whose parents are not in a position to look after them as they should be looked after. I believe that some form of payment should be made to children who find themselves in the condition that they are not able to look after themselves and whose parents are not in a financial position to give them the proper kind of treatment to which they are entitled as Canadian citizens.
I would go even farther. I would say there should be abolition of the means test at the age of sixty-five. To encourage thrift in this country, unless figures can be produced to prove conclusively that the taxpayers cannot afford these suggestions, I am certainly in favour of the abolition of the means test at age sixty-five.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
First of all, with regard to the question put to me by the hon. gentleman whose name indicates the good character of the weather but whose constituency I have forgotten-the hon. member for Battle River- section 10 of the Old Age Pensions Act provides that for the month in which the pensioner dies, the portion of the monthly payment covering that portion of the month in which he was alive may be applied to any debt that may be left unpaid at the time of death.
With regard to the representations that have been made by a number of hon. members with regard to the six-point program of the institute for the blind, may I say I am to be privileged, before this week is out, to have a conference with the managing director of that institute to discuss this and other matters. I must say that I am largely in accord with the general features of what they have asked, at least with regard to the suggestion of separate legislation that will place blind pensioners under legislation that is more properly applicable to them rather than including them, as they are now included, under the provisions of the Old Age Pensions Act.
The committee will appreciate the fact that in the consideration of these matters one must bear in mind a number of things-the general over-all policy of the administration, what one might expect and what one might reasonably say with regard to other features of the act. I will be frank in stating that what I am aiming at is a system of contributory old age pensions in this country.
Having said that, I should add that whatever action we may take in this regard is conditioned and contingent on action on a constitutional basis involving the transference of or agreement on jurisdiction now enjoyed by provincial governments-something that is not as simple as it may appear on the surface to some hon. members. Last November we had a meeting with the provinces and discussed these matters, and any progress we may make in this regard is predicated largely upon the kind of action we may expect from those in authority in the provinces. But as an over-all objective I state unreservedly to the committee that that is my intention, and I am hoping that the progress we have made with the provinces in the matter of health during the past few weeks may be followed by the same measure of collaboration with the provincial governments with respect to old age pensions and welfare matters generally, but particularly old age pensions which involve, if a contributory scheme is to be established, even in connection with a scheme on a co-operative
Supply-Health and Welfare

basis, agreement of some sort as to endowing the central authority with power, that is now enjoyed by the provinces entirely.
With regard to the blind, the amendments we made to the Old Age Pensions Act last session regarding the blind were very considerable in their portent. What we did was to reduce the age from forty to twenty-one, thereby adding no fewer than some twelve hundred blind individuals to the roll of recipients. In other words, twelve hundred blind people are now receiving moneys which, but for those amendments, they would not have received. That is a very considerable matter.
With regard to old age pensions, we are now paying roughly $100 million this year by way of old age pensions. What I said last year I repeat again tonight, that we are looking forward to developing a social security program in this country to cover such things as invalidity and disability which have been mentioned tonight. But we must have a sense of proportion in these things when considering expanding into other important fields of social welfare. Some 65,000 individuals have been added to the list of old age pensioners as a result of the old age pension amendments, and with respect to the $100 million let it not be forgotten that the federal government is paying 75 per cent of the cost of the basic pensions. It is all very well for some hon. members to say the federal government should pay the whole cost; but let me say, without any hesitation or doubt, I do not subscribe to that. The moment you centralize the administration and responsibiEty for all social legislation in the central government, you thereby do to social security and to social welfare and to the provinces a gross injustice, and most of the provinces do not want that. This I can tell hon. members from the discussions I have had with a number of the provinces. I think the present proportion, 75 and 25 per cent, is not an unreasonable proportion.

being ungenerous. I do not say the picture is perfect, but I do not think we are capable of being adjudged as ungenerous.
With regard to the old age pension means test, let this be clearly stated, that our means test is the most liberalized means test of any country in the British commonwealth and, so far as the researches of my officers have gone, of any country in the world.
